slides.title: Inductive bias
slides.content: 3 Inductive bias

slides.title: • Every learning method makes certain assumptions about the data
slides.content: • Every learning method makes certain assumptions about the data • This set of assumptions is called its inductive bias (not to be confused with statistical bias, as in bias-variance) • We illustrate this here for linear regression and decision trees • Important theoretical result: learning without inductive bias is impossible 4 Inductive bias

slides.title: • The linear regression model implicitly assumes:
slides.content: • The linear regression model implicitly assumes: • The effect of each variable on the target is constant (does not depend on other variables) — indeed, if it’s not constant, the interpretation of the mentioned before would be meaningless • The effects of different variables are cumulative (add up) • (there are some more technical assumptions, which do not matter here) • In statistics terminology: “No interaction” bi 7 Important assumptions

slides.content: • After splitting on , each branch is developed entirely independently • may have a positive effect on in one branch, but a negative in another branch • No assumption whatsoever that “ has the same effect everywhere” • From this point of view, decision trees are quite the opposite of linear regression ! slides.title: Trees vs. linear regression
slides.content: 9 Trees vs. linear regression Y = a + b1A + b2S + b2C + b3J On average, professor salaries are 500$ higher than postdoc salaries. I’ll assume the same holds for each country separately. That’s silly! You don’t know that. It may be different in different countries. Nah… I don’t think so. Even if very strong evidence to the contrary is presented, I’ll stick to this assumption. Wow… you’re quite biased! A,S,C,J: Age, Sex, Country, Job

10 Trees vs. linear regression Y = a + b1A + b2S + b2C + b3J Professors earn 500$ more than postdocs if we look at males aged 30-40; males aged 40-50; males aged 50-60; females aged 30-40; females aged 50-60. But what about females aged 40-50? I have no data! Well, surely that’ll be the same, no? I’ll believe that when I see it with my own eyes, not before. You’re quite paranoid!

slides.title: • Which method performs best? Largely depends on your problem!
slides.content: • Which method performs best? Largely depends on your problem! • Each learning approach has an “inductive bias”: implicit assumptions it makes • Learners whose bias fits your problem will perform better • Unfortunately, the problem is often not sufficiently understood to decide in a principled way (neither are learners, in fact!) • “Cumulative effects” vs. “interaction” is just one simple example of how methods can be biased 11 Trees vs. linear regression

slides.title: • Many different machine learning methods exist
slides.content: • Many different machine learning methods exist • They can be used for all kinds of modeling, including predictive modeling • Examples: Naive Bayes, probabilistic graphical models, discriminant analysis, … • All of them have their own bias = implicit assumptions about what properties the true model has • This results in different ways of generalizing towards unseen data • The next slide illustrates this for classification 12 Many methods, many biases

slides.title: • Theoretical proofs exist that bias-free learning is impossible
slides.content: • Theoretical proofs exist that bias-free learning is impossible • Wolpert’s “no free lunch theorems”: For each problem where method A works better than B, there’s a problem where B works better than A (using a probabilistic characterization). There is no single best method for learning. • A less technical argument (presented by Mitchell, 1996): • Let hypothesis space = set of all hypotheses that the learner will consider, and version space = subset of consistent with the training set • What happens if contains every possible concept (i.e., every imaginable function from to {True,False}? • Then for any hypothesis that predicts True for a new instance , there exists a that predicts False for (just choose for all and ). • Hence, if we let all vote, the votes will be exactly 50-50 for every unseen instance • General conclusion: no generalization towards unseen cases is possible without making some assumptions ℋ VS ℋ ℋ X h ∈VS q h′￼∈VS q h′￼(x) = h(x) x ≠q h′￼(q) = ¬h(q) h ∈VS 14 Get rid of bias?

slides.title: • Bias can be in the form of preference or selection bias
slides.content: • Bias can be in the form of preference or selection bias • Selection bias: not every imaginable hypothesis is in the hypothesis space • Preference bias: some hypotheses in the hypothesis space are preferred over others • e.g., decision trees: preference for small trees over large ones • In the remainder, we will focus on selection bias • The closer a hypothesis space is to being able to represent every imaginable hypothesis, the smaller the inductive bias is • How can we measure the strength of the bias, and how does it impact learnability? 15 Bias
16 Measuring the expressiveness, or “capacity”, of a hypothesis space

slides.title: • Hypothesis space
slides.content: • Hypothesis space : set of all models (“hypotheses”) that could be returned by the learner • We will here focus on predictive models (functions ) • Question: How expressive / flexible is a given hypothesis space? Can it model a wide variety of functions / concepts, or a rather limited set? • One way to answer this question is the following: given a dataset , can we always find a model that perfectly fits it (i.e., for all )? How large should be before this is no longer the case? • This expresses ’s “capacity to perfectly fit” data • Note: this also implies a capacity to overfit data • We simply call it the capacity of the hypothesis space ℋ f : 𝒳→𝒴 D f f(x) = y (x, y) ∈D D ℋ 17 Capacity of a hypothesis space

slides.title: • PAC stands for “probably approximately correct”
slides.content: • PAC stands for “probably approximately correct” • Assume examples are drawn randomly from one distribution ( i.i.d. : independently and identically distributed) • We can never guarantee that a correct hypothesis is learned: there’s always a small chance that randomly drawn examples are highly unrepresentative • Therefore, relax the learning task: learner should very probably find an approximately correct hypothesis • Formally: with probability , return a hypothesis with accuracy • The smaller and are chosen, the stronger this “soft guarantee” is ≥1 −δ ≥1 −ε δ ε 28 PAC learning

slides.title: • Formal definition of PAC-learnability according to Mitchell (1997):
slides.content: • Formal definition of PAC-learnability according to Mitchell (1997): • Assume a class C of possible target concepts defined over instance space X; instances have “size” n; learner uses hypothesis space • C is PAC-learnable by using if for all c in C, for all probability distributions over X, and for all 0<δ<1/2 and 0<ε<1/2, the following holds: finds with probability 1-δ some with acc( f ) ≥ 1-ε in time polynomial in 1/δ, 1/ε, n and size(c) L ℋ L ℋ L f ∈ℋ 29 PAC-learnability

slides.title: • Sample complexity relates the chances of successful learning to the size of the
slides.content: • Sample complexity relates the chances of successful learning to the size of the training set • The sample complexity of a learning problem is related to the expressiveness of the hypothesis space • The latter can be formally expressed by measures such as the size of the hypothesis space (for finite sizes), its VC-dimension, and its Rademacher complexity 37 Summary

slides.title: • PAC-learning assumes random sampling. It does not say anything about
slides.content: • PAC-learning assumes random sampling. It does not say anything about learning settings where the instances are carefully chosen by a benevolent teacher, or by the learner, to be maximally informative (e.g., the active learning setting) • Sample complexity is only one measure. Computational complexity is another possibly useful measure: how much computation is needed, rather than how much data 38 Some final remarks…
